raw_response:
*Thinking as the farmer in her own voice...*

---

Ai-yo, 五亩半地 (five and a half mu)... not much, but it's what my husband and I can still manage at our age. Stevia (甜叶菊) has been good to us — the company from the town sends someone in spring with the seedlings, and they buy back the dry leaves in fall. No need to worry about selling, which is a blessing. My neighbor 老李 started growing it before us, maybe seven, eight years ago, and when I saw his granddaughter going to school with new clothes I thought — we should try this too.

The plants I have now are in their second year. I put them in the ground last spring. If you take care of them, they can give you leaves for three, four years before you need to pull them up and plant again. So this year I don't need to buy new seedlings, thank heavens — that money I can save.

Here's how I think about this year:

**Spring preparation.** When the weather warms up in late March, I'll go over the field with a hoe, clean out the dead stalks from last winter, break up the crust. I can't rent a tractor for 5.5 mu — too small, too expensive, and the company's stevia rows are too close together for a big machine anyway. My husband and I do it by hand, slowly. Takes us maybe a week.

**Fertilizer.** Before the plants really wake up, I'll spread compound fertilizer — 复合肥 — the kind with the green bag from the shop at the crossroads. Last year I put down about two bags on the whole field. That felt right. Plants were a nice dark green all summer. I'll do the same this year. Maybe two bags and a bit more if I have the money. Then after the first cutting in early summer, I put down some urea (尿素) to help them grow back fast — one bag, spread thin, right before irrigation so it soaks in. After the second cutting I sprinkle a little more urea if the leaves look yellow. If they look fine, I save it.

I don't know these English numbers they ask about, potassium this and that. I buy 复合肥 — that already has everything in it, the shopkeeper told me so. And 尿素 is 尿素. That's what I know.

**Water.** The well is shared with three other families. We take turns. Stevia likes water but not too much — if the roots sit wet, the leaves go bad. I irrigate right after planting wakes up in spring, then maybe after each cutting, and one more time if July and August are dry. Maybe four times in the year. Each turn at the well costs money for the electricity — you pay by the hour. I watch the sky before I turn on the pump.

**Pests.** Stevia doesn't have many big problems. Aphids sometimes, in early summer. I can see them on the underside of the leaves when I bend down to look. If I see them I buy a small bottle of the spray from the shop — my son-in-law reads the label for me and tells me how much to mix. I don't spray unless I see the bugs. Waste of money otherwise. Weeds — I pull them by hand. My back isn't good but 5.5 mu I can still manage, with my husband helping.

**Harvest.** Two cuttings for sure, maybe three if the fall stays warm. First cut is around the end of June, just before the flowers open — the company man told us years ago, leaves are sweetest then. Cut with a small sickle, spread on the ground or on a tarp to dry in the sun, two or three days. Then I bag them up and the truck comes. Second cut in late August, same way. If September is warm, I might get a small third cut in October, but the leaves are thinner then.

**Labor.** It's just me and the old man. Our daughter lives in Handan, she can't come for harvest — she's working. If we can't keep up with the cutting, I ask my younger brother's wife to help for a few days, and I pay her with some cash and a meal. At 5.5 mu we can mostly handle it ourselves. Slowly, slowly.

**What I worry about.** The company's buying price. Last year it was a little lower than the year before. My neighbor says he heard they might pay even less this year because the market is soft. I can't do anything about that — I just grow good leaves and hope. If the price drops too much, next year maybe I'll think about something else. But this year the plants are already in the ground, so I carry on.

That's the plan. Same as last year, more or less. When you've farmed 40 years you learn — don't change too many things at once.
